en: A Brief Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, Scroll 30.
Record on the Beginning of the "Ten Stages" Chapter.
There are three reasons for the introduction of this chapter: first, to answer the preceding questions in sequence; second, to present the causes that correspond to the fruition; third...
The various practices support one another,
as stated in the thirty-sixth fascicle of the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra.
How can each and every point be answered in detail?
This chapter is likewise the great main body of an entire section;
it extends from what precedes to what follows.
He answered each question one by one in sequence;
this is also the fundamental basis of this entire treatise.
Thus are the forty-two great questions as mentioned above.
Question: Regarding the sequential order of the scriptural passages on the practice of cause and effect, the initial inquiry within the section on causes states:
"The ten abodes, the ten practices, the ten transferences, the ten treasuries, the ten stages, the ten vows, the ten concentrations, the ten masteries, and the ten summits."
They all answered according to the sequence of the text:
the Ten Abodes were taught on the summit of Mount Sumeru,
and the Ten Practices were taught in the Yāma Heaven.
The Tuṣita Heaven speaks of the ten dedications;
the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven speaks of the ten stages.
The Brahmajāla Sūtra says:
The people of the Five Indies speak of ten dhyānas.
The *Yingluo* also says:
"While I was in the third dhyāna, I gathered the eight dhyānas."
Various accounts state that there are one hundred trillion verses on the samādhi of the stage of being born only once more before Buddhahood (*ekajātipratibaddha*).
For now, I shall briefly explain a single verse.
Furthermore, the fourth chapter, "Explaining the Meaning" (*Arthaviniścaya*), states:
While I was in the fourth dhyāna,
I taught eighty million Brahmā devas that the Tathāgata Śāntaprabha is without mind and without form, yet he serenely illumines all things.
If one were to rely on this meaning, the extensive text of this assembly would consist of one hundred and eight thousand verses.
Furthermore, the Brahmajāla Sūtra states:
"In the Hall of Sublime Light, the ten worlds were expounded;
in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the ten abodes were expounded."
The Yāma Heaven speaks of the ten practices;
the Tuṣita Heaven speaks of dedication;
the Nirmāṇarati Heaven speaks of the ten patiences.
The ten meditations and ten vows, as well as the four meditations, are explained in the "Chapter on the Dharma Gate of Vairocana’s Mind-Ground.
The remaining thousands and hundreds of Śākyamunis are likewise the same.
Furthermore, there are the four heavens, the ten treasuries, the ten masteries, and the ten summits, along with the verses spoken upon ascending to heaven.
Because there is no textual passage in such scriptures as the *Prabhāsa-prabhāvanā-sūtra* [or *Ratnolkā-dhāraṇī-sūtra*] that addresses this, the citations here are not exhaustive.
As for what was previously called the "Ten Treasuries" (*daśakośa*),
it was intended to establish the meaning of the practice (*caryā*).
As in the fifth dedication,
the ten treasuries (daśakośa) are subsequently explained;
these are the treasuries that constitute the dedication itself, and thus they answer the preceding question.
Therefore, it is known that this is not an answer to the previous question regarding the ten illuminations being identical to the ten vajras.
Furthermore, there are also passages where these two chapters, "Illumination" and "Patience," are explained in this manner.

From the *Saṃghāṭa-sūtra* downward, the three grades of the mind-king serve as the presiding host; the quantities, dwellings, and lands are unlike those in the heavens, and thus this should be explained as referring to the human realm.
These ten stages (daśabhūmi) are established as ten by way of the dharmas of impartial salvation;
a detailed explanation follows below in the section on the fundamental divisions.
Furthermore, there are the meanings of the eight precautions, the sixteen aspects, and so forth, as well as the five patiences and others.
However, the meaning of these involves immeasurable and great firmness.
Furthermore, these do not exceed two kinds of wisdom:
namely, ultimate wisdom (bhūta-jñāna) and skillful means wisdom (upāya-jñāna),
which are also termed realized wisdom (sākṣāt-kriyā-jñāna) and object-illuminating wisdom (ālambana-pratibhāsa-jñāna).
It is also called the two paths of realization and teaching;
it is also called the non-abiding assistance of realization;
and it is also called the four measures of wisdom and the three types of merit and wisdom.
Such immeasurable and boundless virtues and titles as these—
if one were to follow the various things from which they are freed, they would likewise be immeasurable.
As for what is called "real wisdom":
The true realization in which object and wisdom are both fused into non-duality constitutes ultimate wisdom (*paramārtha-jñāna*).
The six perfections and four means of integration, though distinguished by their myriad varieties across different stages, constitute expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*).
These two meanings encompass all practices and virtues without exception.
There are no stages that do not accumulate [merit and wisdom], yet their essence and function differ;
taken collectively, they constitute ten numbers, beginning with the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā*) and culminating in the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā*).
Nevertheless, as the meanings of essence and function diverge, they further comprise eight types.
First, by the distinction of hindrances;
second, by the classification according to training;
third, by the division according to understanding.
Fourth, by means of practice;
fifth, by means of indicating retribution;
sixth, by means of citing analogies.
Seventh, the quantity by which they are summarized;
eighth, the uniformity of the view of equality.
First, regarding the ten obstacles:
First, the obstacle of the mark of selfhood in ordinary beings;
second, the obstacle of engaging in erroneous conduct toward the bodies and so forth of sentient beings;
third, the obstacle of the mark of darkness, which is the false obscuration regarding the various dharmas of hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
Fourth, the obstacle of pride regarding the understanding of the Dharma;
fifth, the obstacle of the pride of self-purity;
sixth, the obstacle of the habitual tendencies of subtle afflictions.
Seventh, the obstacle of the habitual tendencies of subtle marks;
eighth, the obstacle of having practice despite the absence of marks;
ninth, the obstacle of being unable to skillfully benefit sentient beings.
Tenth, among all phenomena, one does not encounter self-obstruction.
Therefore, one cultivates the remedial practices of the ten stages, such as the remedies for the afflictions and so forth.
This is the classification according to training.
Regarding the classification of the stages:
the ten great vows of the first stage;
the training in ethical discipline of the second stage.
The third stage is the training in meditative concentration.
From the fourth stage to the seventh stage is the training in wisdom for one's own benefit.
From the eighth stage upward is the training in wisdom for the benefit of others.

Regarding the Middle Way Chapter on the Perfection of Self-Benefit, there are the contemplations of the Truths, dependent origination, and the study of true signlessness; the factors of enlightenment of the fifth stage, and the four kinds of purity.
Among these, the purity of aspiration pertains to the first stage.
Second is the two stages of higher ethical discipline;
third is the three stages of higher mind;
fourth is the purification of higher wisdom.
These are subsumed within the fourth through the seventh stages (*bhūmi*).
Among the activities for the benefit of others, they consist of the three types of action (*karman*).
Furthermore, among these, generosity, ethical discipline, and patience constitute the preeminent ethical discipline (*adhiśīla*).
Training in meditation is the higher mental state (*adhyāśaya*);
training in wisdom and training in diligence encompass all three types of wisdom.

These comprise the twelve stages of abiding: the stage of the spiritual lineage (*gotra-vihāra*) is subsumed by hearing; the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā-vihāra*) is subsumed by reflection; and the ten stages (*daśa-bhūmi*) along with their preliminary practices and the extensive fruit (*vipula-phala*) are subsumed by cultivation.
Regarding the terms "understanding" and "differentiation":
the first stage is called faith,
and up to the tenth stage, they are designated as the ten kinds of wisdom.
The "Great" [Vehicle] may also consist of five patiences (kṣānti) or fourteen patiences, involving the vision of the truths and the path of cultivation (darśana- and bhāvanā-mārga).
As for what is called "practice" (caryā),
the first stage (bhūmi) is designated as dāna (giving).
Up to the tenth stage is called "knowledge.
Regarding the four reliances and the four fruits,
as for what is termed "retribution and manifestation":
The first stage is that of the King of Jambudvīpa,
up to the tenth stage, which is that of the Heavenly King Maheśvara.
As for the metaphors used to illustrate this:
The first stage is like refining gold with fire;
continuing thus through the tenth stage, it becomes an ornament for the crown of the Lord of the Gods (Īśvara).
It is the same for the jewels from the neck, the head, the ponds, the mountains, and the seas.
If one speaks in terms of numerical quantity,
at the first stage (bhūmi) one attains one hundred samādhis,
and so on, until at the tenth stage one attains as many samādhis as there are atoms in ten unspeakably many thousands of myriads of koṭis of nayutas of Buddha-worlds.
Regarding the "single observation" of Yi and Qi:

it is spoken of in terms of the functioning of non-discriminative realized wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), which is eternally quiescent; the practices of all stages (*bhūmi*) are said to be beyond calculation, for the essence of this wisdom is profound and vast.
Such quiescence of principle constitutes a single contemplation.
As for what is now called "earth," it is because when a bodhisattva resolves their mind, they bear the burden [of sentient beings] like the earth.
The *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* states:
"The prajñā that enters into principle is called 'abiding'; that which gives rise to merit is called 'ground' (*bhūmi*).
Nāgārjuna’s commentary explains:
"Bhūmi" (ground) refers to the stages and abodes of the bodhisattva; it is called "ground" because it serves as their dwelling place.
The *Ratnavyuha Sūtra* states:
"Bhūmi means that which sustains millions of asaṃkhyeya merits."
It also brings about the production of all causes, effects, and meritorious virtues.
The conduct of the Mahāsattva is profound, vast, and difficult to fathom, possessing four meanings like the earth.
First, his noble conduct is deep, thick, and expansive; it is firm and indestructible.
Second, it causes the myriad things to grow and flourish.
Third, it bears the weight of all things like the earth.
Fourth, it operates upon things without emotional attachment, as illustrated by the analogies of the earth, fire, wind, and so forth.
The practice of the bodhisattva is likewise;
according to the explanation provided in the treatise,
it is divided into eight sections within the first stage (*bhūmi*).
1. The introductory section (nidāna-bhāga).
2. The section on samādhi (samādhi-bhāga).
3. The section on suchness (tathatā-bhāga).
4. The Section on Arising;
5. The Section on the Main Body;
6. The Section on Requesting.
Regarding the seventh section,
the "Comparison of Superiority," the treatise’s exposition of the eight aspects refers exclusively to the first stage (*bhūmi*) and does not apply to all ten stages.
If one follows the preceding analysis, there are three parts in the subsequent section:
first, from the beginning up to the description of extending the right hand to rub the crown of the head, which constitutes the introductory exposition;
second, from the arising from samādhi up to the parable of the mani-jewel, which is the second part, the main exposition.
The third section, from "From the Moving Ground, Raining Flowers" onwards, clarifies the circulation and the manifest testimony.
Within this, according to the sequence of the first three assemblies, there should be six segments;
however, this chapter consists of three sentences.
This refers to three aspects: the assembly taking their seats, entering meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and the omission of the offering of alms, verses of praise, and the emission of light.

Following the introductory sequence of the preceding assembly, the entry into the "Section on the Arising of the Fundamental" (*mūla-bhāga*) universally enumerates ten figures for both persons and dharmas.
It serves as the general foundation for the stages of abiding, practice, and progression (*caryā-bhūmi*).
Within this, although the ten names have already been requested collectively and individually— corresponding to the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*)—
it is only from the "General Preface" (*sāmānyanirdeśa*) onwards that the ten specific meanings are revealed individually.
Yet the treatise states:
"The first stage has eight [sections] because the names of the beginning and end overlap; the positions are mixed, and the general and specific are combined.
The first three constitute the introduction, and the next three provide a general exposition."
The first [of these] corresponds to the "correct exposition," while the latter two correspond to "scriptural authority" (*āgama-pramāṇa*).
This constitutes the analysis of the meaning within the first stage (*bhūmi*).
However, regarding the subsequent nine stages, there are both points of convergence and divergence.
The individual invitations prior to the various lower stages are not of this same category.
Based on the current division, looking back at what was previously called "that time," one must possess the aforementioned nine virtues.
Because the multitude of sages pay him increased reverence, he is called the World-Honored One (Bhagavān).
The meaning of "Bhaga" is explained extensively in the treatises.
As the treatise states:
Because it demonstrates superiority through the comparison of time, place,
and so forth— specifically by teaching this at the initial time and in a superior location, such as this palace—
the excellence of the place is thus termed "superiority of place."
Why is it not called the "Non-Form Realm"? This place is so designated because of the ripening of karmic results.
Why is it that during the first seven days, one does not speak of the causal conditions for the practice of contemplation?
Because his original purpose was to practice for the sake of attaining enlightenment for the benefit of others,
he did not speak for seven days while contemplating this;
it was to demonstrate that he was experiencing the great joy of the Dharma.
For what reason is his own joy in the Dharma revealed?
It is to cause sentient beings to increase their love and reverence toward the Tathāgata.

Contemplating the causal conditions of practice, he reveals the uncommon dharmas (*āveṇika-dharma*), which are alternative names for the dharmas of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) and those still in training (*śaikṣa*). These are the uncommon dharmas.
It has already been shown that when enumerating the locations, this single assembly is not the only one.
In the preceding five assemblies, there were times and places where [the teaching] did not arise at the Bodhi Tree;
yet, while the six heavens were simultaneous and even throughout the ten directions, the time was the same while the locations differed.
It may also be simultaneous and in the same location.
There are four permutations regarding location, simultaneity, and difference in time and difference in location.
Regarding the statement here that "it is not recited for seven days":
These words were spoken precisely at the moment of his initial attainment of perfect enlightenment.
This matter should have been examined previously in the section on the Vajra-ground;
the same applies to all the assemblies.
Regarding the statement that "the time and place are superior" to manifest the superiority of the Dharma:
is it not the case that the teachings of the previous assemblies were also superior?
The same applies to the preceding [passages] regarding the seven days not speaking.
Some say this is merely a scriptural measure of the Hīnayāna;
such a textual passage does not exist within the Mahāyāna *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*.
Regarding the second section, there are two parts:
first, the praise of virtues;
second, the enumeration of the assembly.
Within the praise of virtues, there are two parts.
First, four sections that generally praise the virtues of his own practice and his external transformation of others.
Second, a summary of the virtues of these two types of practice.
Regarding the first of the four [sections], which praises virtues in general:
it first praises the virtues of the self-cultivation of the long-established assembly in this region.
These bodhisattvas represent this region.
"All Bodhisattvas" refers to those from other directions;
they may also be called the assembly of those born together and those born separately.

By mentioning these two assemblies together, [the text] praises both their own and others' virtues regarding the two types of practice: that which pertains to themselves and that which pertains to others.
"Entering" refers to understanding and realization;
it means exhausting one's thought to achieve universal illumination.
"Skillfully able," and so forth, praises the virtue of external transformation.
The reason why the Great Being first accumulates merit for himself is that he seeks to preserve the essential means of benefiting others and transforming sentient beings;
since these depend solely upon supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), they are explained next.
Regarding the sphere of wisdom:
among the ten thousand practices of the Great Being, wisdom is primary; therefore, it is praised first.
From "Having fulfilled his vows" onwards is the second cycle of praising his virtues.
Regarding the phrase "obstructing the practice," this refers to both the practices and the vows;
thus, these practices and vows praise both [the previous and current] stages, as both possess practices and vows.
Bodhisattvas accomplish all practices through their vows;
this is explained because the vow is the foundation of practice.
"All worlds" refers collectively to the three types of worlds.
"All kalpas" refers collectively to the temporal divisions within the three periods of time;
these are all cited as temporal divisions for the purpose of accomplishing practice.
The same applies to the lands, which likewise involve kalpas of varying lengths.
All lands and regions are the realms transformed by the King;
he constantly cultivates all practices of the bodhisattvas,
pervading the world and all kalpas without exception.
There is no land where they do not penetrate;
they cultivate the bodhisattva practices in all such times and places.
Because time is protracted and space is vast, their wisdom and conduct are likewise boundless.
Regarding the inexhaustibility of merit and wisdom:
because the practices of a bodhisattva do not exceed these two— merit and wisdom—
it is sufficient to clarify only these two.
"To be able to bring benefit to all" refers to external transformation (*bāhya-pariṇāmanā*).
What was previously termed "supernormal powers" (*abhijñā*) is here termed "benefit."
This is merely a mutual expression of profound lamentation.
From the point of "ability" until the end, it leads toward the gate of Nirvana;
this constitutes the third cycle, clarifying both self-cultivation and external transformation.
Regarding the Bodhisattva’s wisdom and skillful means:
taking the ultimate as true wisdom and grasping the conventional as skillful means.
One teaching states that when wisdom takes emptiness as its object and knows it as being like space, it is called "true wisdom" (prajñā).
To know this yet not be attached to it is called "skillful means" (upāya).
These two forms of wisdom are the parents of perfect enlightenment.
Because it illuminates and realizes the nature of all practices through their essential strength, it reaches that ultimate shore;
its ability to cause sentient beings to turn their backs on birth-and-death and head toward nirvana constitutes external transformation (*bāhya-vinaya*).
Birth and death are ultimate suffering, while Nirvana is ultimate bliss.
To cause sentient beings to turn their backs on suffering and reach bliss,
the transformations that move them and the gates through which they pass are all said to be capable of providing passage.
From "never ceasing the wheel of Dharma" is the fourth cycle,
clarifying the practice of benefiting oneself and others.
This refers to never ceasing any of the practices undertaken by bodhisattvas.
This summarizes all practices in general.
From "from meditative concentration" up to "clear wisdom" is the detailed explanation of various practices.
The section beginning with "all that is performed" clarifies external transformation.
Within this, there are two cycles that clarify the three types of action (*trikarma*).
The first briefly explains the body; from "below this" onwards, it is explained extensively; and from "thus" onwards, it is a summary.
Regarding the phrase "skillfully able to manifest":
He demonstrates his own practice to sentient beings;
now, by emulating and practicing it, his every movement becomes a model for all things, and thus he is said to be "skillfully able.
This refers to the non-active divine power (*anabhisaṃskāra-ṛddhi*).
Non-conception constitutes the spirit.
Because the mind merges with the true mark (dharmatā), its form can reach everywhere.
It is also said that there is no agent.
It is not a matter of deliberate mental effort.
As with those from the eighth stage upward, they act spontaneously according to their nature without relying on deliberate mental effort.
Being able to reach the ten directions, they arrive there by mere thought; they exhort [the Buddhas] to preach the Dharma, and the ten directions receive benefit.
Therefore, this is external transformation (*bāhya-vikṛti*).
Reverently upholding the Dharma without forgetting it constitutes reception (*pratigraha*).
It is also said that the preceding four pairs constitute specific praises.
The section beginning with "Always with great compassion" and following summarizes the four pairs.
Regarding these four: first, wisdom serves as the means for the commencement of practice, while supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) serve as the basis for transforming sentient beings;
thus, wisdom and supernatural powers constitute one pair.
Second, it manifests that what is accomplished within oneself benefits others;
this refers to the mutual relationship between the internal and the external.
Third, it begins with understanding and culminates in reaching the other shore.
It enables sentient beings to first turn their backs on birth and death and ultimately return to nirvana;
this is explained in terms of the beginning and the end being relative to one another.
Fourth, because the practice is uninterrupted, and the receiving and accepting [of the teachings] are not abandoned.
To be able to constantly practice the One Vehicle to extensively save all classes of beings is precisely the fourth [point], which corresponds to benefiting others for one's own benefit.
From "Thus" onwards is the fifth [point], which summarizes and praises the preceding four.
This is the second name listed among the assembly following Vajragarbha.
Since this Bodhisattva is the leader who requested the teaching in the fourth assembly, his name is listed first.
The treatise asks: "For what reason does only Vajragarbha speak [this]?
The commentary explains:
"All afflictions are difficult to destroy, yet this Dharma can shatter them; its roots of goodness are firm and solid, just like a vajra."
Therefore, it is spoken of by a name that is not different [from its nature]. Why is he named Vajragarbha?
"Garbha" (matrix/store) signifies firmness; it is like the core of a tree, or like a fetus dwelling within a womb.
For this reason, it is called "firm as a diamond.
Among all roots of goodness, its power is supreme, like a diamond;
because it can generate and bring forth the roots of goodness for practice in the realms of humans and devas, and cannot be destroyed by them, it is named the "Diamond Treasury" (Vajragarbha).
The following thirty-seven bodhisattvas are named according to their immeasurable virtues and are presented by way of testimony.
The introduction has already been explained;
from the entry into samādhi below is the main body of the text.
This is the second member of samādhi (*samādhyaṅga*).
According to the various assemblies, it corresponds to the sixth passage on entering meditative absorption (*praveśasamādhi*) within the introduction.
It contains two meanings.
First, entering meditative concentration; second, explaining the entry into concentration. Within the explanation, there are three parts:
first, the reason for entering concentration, which corresponds to the content of the initial phrase;
second, from "desiring to proclaim" onwards, clarifying the purpose of the concentration.
From "Third, having finished the explanation" onwards, it clarifies what is empowered by meditative concentration;
this is the third empowerment section,
specifically termed the "empowerment of the three karmas."
If one follows the commentary on the initial entry into meditative absorption,
this corresponds to the "limb of samādhi";
from the phrase "at that very moment" onwards, it corresponds to the "added limb."
Therein are three points:
first, that the preparatory signs (*prayoga-nimitta*) reveal the three karmas, which is the reason for entering meditative absorption;
second, as to why the preparatory stage is described with the phrase "for the sake of benefiting oneself and others," this refers to the purpose of what follows.
Third, what is "empowerment" (adhiṣṭhāna)? It refers to the empowerment of speech, mind, and body.

Following the section on eloquent exposition, there are forty phrases which constitute the characteristics of empowerment; among these, five phrases clarify the characteristics of the empowerment of the three karmas.
First, the passage beginning with "In each of the ten directions, beyond ten billion buddha-fields... clarifies the characteristics of the empowerment of the three karmas.
First is physical action (*kāyakarman*), next is verbal action (*vākkarman*), and next is mental action (*manaskarman*).
From "by the majestic power of the Buddhas of the twenty directions" onwards,
it is explained that the empowerment is due to the power of the original vows of a single Buddha.
From "The four majestic powers" (*catur-vaiśāradya*) downward, [the text] adds [these] because they manifest supernatural power (*ṛddhi-bala*).
From "You possess... downward, it clarifies the internal cause (*adhyātma-hetu*).
The preceding four are the conditions (*pratyaya*).
The fifth is the characteristic of being augmented by the harmony of causes and conditions.
Regarding the frequent mention of Buddhas augmenting [the teaching],
it is to manifest the increase of a heart of reverence for both the Dharma and the Dharma-preacher.
To speak plainly, this is out of reverence for the person and respect for the Dharma.
Why is he given the same title, Vajragarbha?
It is because of the power of his original vow.

This samādhi is the essence of the Dharma; when he was practicing as a bodhisattva, he taught this Dharma together [with others], and now that he has attained perfect enlightenment, he is also named Vajragarbha.
Thus, there is no difference between the names; it is an empowerment (adhiṣṭhāna).

Because there are bodhisattvas who, having heard that all Tathāgatas share their own name, experience an increase in joy equal to the number of ten buddha-fields; for this reason, the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are taught to them.
Thus, it is because of these many explanations of the number ten that [this teaching exists].
Regarding the passage beginning with "desiring to proclaim all [that has been taught]," the treatise asks:
"For what purpose is this addition made?
This refers to the twenty phrases concerning the objective for entering meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
The first ten [perfections] are for one's own benefit and the latter ten are for the benefit of others; thus they are added.
"All bodhisattvas" refers to those abiding on the stage of practice through faith (*śraddhācaryābhūmi*).
The inconceivable qualities of all Buddhas are the supramundane factors of enlightenment;
they are seen, known, and realized by the wise.
"Entering" means gaining realization through faith and delight.
"The stage of wisdom" refers to the wisdom of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), as explained in the "Fundamental Section.
This single phrase constitutes the fundamental summary of the entry.
If one relies on the root, "all bodhisattvas" is the general [statement],
while the subsequent phrase, "having entered the stage of wisdom," and so forth,
constitutes the specific [details]. Based on the root, there are nine distinct entries for entering.
First, by being subsumed within the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*), one gathers all roots of goodness;

second, by entering the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) through reflecting on their meaning, one skillfully discerns all Buddha-dharmas among all the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*).
Third, because of the extensive knowledge of dharmas through the mutual penetration of the three natures;
fourth, because of entering into the teaching of all dharmas through definitive exposition for the sake of conversion;
fifth, because of realizing and entering non-conceptual wisdom.
Sixth, because they enter into the non-negligence that cannot be defiled by worldly dharmas;
seventh, because they progressively enter each stage through the purification of the root of goodness of non-attachment;
eighth, because Bodhisattvas exhaustively enter into the attainment of inconceivable power of wisdom.
Ninth, because the Buddha has fully entered the realm of wisdom of those who have attained all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*).
Furthermore,
it is said that these ten phrases correspond to the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
If one's own practice is thus,
so too is the external transformation of others.
How is this known?
Regarding the ten phrases at the beginning, it is stated at the end that they "expound the distinctions of the ten bodhisattva stages (bodhisattvabhūmi) as they truly are.

According to the commentary, these are treated as a general summary of the primary subject matter, which is then correlated with the three types of wisdom (*prajñā*) and the ten entries (*daśapraveśa*); however, this correlation does not appear to correspond to the [ten] stages.

These bases (*āyatana*) represent a progressive sequence of increasingly superior distinctions in the meaning of the analytical knowledge; it should be understood that within each of the ten phrases concerning the fundamental bases, there are six kinds of distinctions that correspondingly apply.
Sixth are the general characteristics, the specific characteristics, the dissimilar characteristics, the characteristic of formation, and the characteristic of destruction.
"General" refers to the fundamental entrance;
"specific" refers to the remaining nine entrances.
Because they enter into the same characteristic;
because the different ones increase the characteristic.
This is a brief explanation of the characteristic of establishment.
The characteristics of destruction are explained in detail;
thus, they are like the formation and destruction of the world-system.
This refers only to the differences between the general and specific, the entry into increase, and the concise and extensive expositions.
The subsequent ten phrases concern the attainment of the distinctions of the ten stages through the practice of benefiting others.
In the *Mahāvaipulya* [version], there are eleven phrases:
the first is general, while the latter ten are specific.
The treatise on the sūtra also consists of eleven phrases.
The first phrase, concerning the beginning and end of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), summarizes the distinctions among the ten stages; the ten phrases following it provide the specific details.
One should understand that these do not correspond exactly to the *Mahāvaipulya* version.
Within the [section on] "Distinctions," there are ten phrases:
the first five concern one's own practice, and the latter five concern external transformation.
The treatise explains that these encompass the benefits [of the preceding section].
The final five sciences (*vidyāsthāna*) are able to encompass benefit.
By composing this commentary as a basis for exposition, one attains ten kinds of beginning and end.
As the treatise says:
That which begins with faith, the desire to draw near, and so forth,
and concludes with the mindfulness and upholding of the various stages (*bhūmi*),
is further characterized as "faith" because it accords with the Buddha-dharma through both scriptural authority (*āgama*) and realized conviction (*adhigama*), being necessarily certain.
"Desire" (chanda) refers to the aspiration for the sublime Dharma based on faith; thus it is called desire.
"Approaching" (upaniṣad) means aspiring to draw near to the Buddha to hear the Dharma.
"Ultimate" (niṣṭhā) refers to mindfulness and retention, which is to say, the accumulation of merit.
Furthermore, there are both scripture (*āgama*) and realization (*adhigama*).
Scripture is the beginning and realization is the end;
alternatively, scripture may be considered the teaching.
The "realization" (pramāṇa) refers to wisdom as the general [category], while the others are the specific [categories].
Among the ten types of beginning and end,
there are eleven sūtra texts.
The first two phrases constitute the general summary, while the [subsequent] nine phrases constitute the detailed exposition.

First, regarding the "comprehension of the beginning and end" (*ādyantasaṃgraha*), the first two phrases collectively summarize the preceding section as the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*); this is because one receives, maintains, and explains the Dharma according to what has been heard.
As it is said in the Sūtra according to reality, this is because of the skillful means that distinguish the ten stages (*bhūmi*) of a bodhisattva.
The *Mahāvaipulya* states:
"Because the bodhisattva dwells securely in the ten stages."
Second, they desire to abide in accordance with the ten stages from beginning to end.
Third, they practice from beginning to end by preaching the untainted Dharma.
Fourth, they realize from beginning to end the light of great wisdom—the wisdom of selflessness—adorned with sovereign mastery.
"Radiance" refers to its opposition to primordial ignorance (*ādyavidyā*).
It is the "Gate of Fulfillment" because it enters the beginning and end of the fivefold path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
As the treatise states:
In this regard, there are five kinds of obstacles for a bodhisattva:
first, the obstacle of being unable to refute various heterodox arguments;
second, the obstacle of being unable to answer difficult challenges.
Third is the obstacle of attachment to the Lesser Vehicle;
fourth is the obstacle of indolence in transforming sentient beings;
fifth is the obstacle of lacking the wisdom of skillful means.
The antidotes to these obstacles have five stages from beginning to end.
First is the stage of being able to destroy the obstacle of false doctrines;
as it is said in the Sūtra, they are taught in successive order according to where they should be applied.
Second, they are able to answer difficult questions from beginning to end,
because they have attained the light of unimpeded eloquence and are fully endowed with the stage of great unimpeded wisdom.
Third, the beginning and end of the antidote to attachment to the Lesser Vehicle,
because one does not lose the bodhisattva mind.
Fourth, the beginning and end of the antidote for transforming sentient beings.
Because it brings to maturity and transforms all realms of sentient beings.
Fifth, the wisdom of skillful means counteracts the beginning and the end;
it is the thorough penetration and discernment of the five fields of knowledge (*pañcavidyāsthāna*).
Because one attains the definitive knowledge that reaches all places. What is empowerment?
It refers to empowerment by means of speech, mind, and body.
What is empowerment by speech?
Because these ten stages are explained through verbal activity (*vākkarman*),
they are placed at the beginning in order to express and manifest the underlying principle.
As the *Mahāvaipulya* states:
Regarding your request that I explain the distinctions of this Dharma-gate:
they refer to the distinctions of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*),
which arise from their various names and characteristics.
Based on the fundamental basis of vocal action, eloquence is of two kinds.
The first is eloquence through the power of others,
which means that by relying on the Buddha's spiritual power, one is not obscured.
Second, there are four types of eloquence through one's own power:
first, eloquence of action,
because one's own roots of goodness are pure.
Second is the eloquence of non-action,
because of the pure dharma-realm.
Third is the eloquence of transforming sentient beings.
For the sake of benefiting sentient beings, there is the fourth:
pure eloquence of body (*kāya-viśuddhi-pratibhāna*).
Within this purity of body, three kinds of exhaustion (*kṣaya*) are manifested.
First, the Bodhisattva;
second, the non-exhaustion of the two vehicles;
third, the exhaustion of the Buddha.
There are three types for Bodhisattvas,
two types for those of the Two Vehicles,
and one type for Buddhas.
Combined with the six types,
the four types previously mentioned regarding self and others constitute ten types in total.
Regarding the three kinds of bodhisattvas:
first, the bodhisattva who has reached the ultimate end.
This is because the dharma-body is free from mind, mentation, and consciousness, and the dharma-body is the support for wisdom alone; it is the body of wisdom.
Second is the benefit of present retribution,
because one receives the prediction of enlightenment from all Buddhas.
Third is the benefit of future retribution.
Because one attains a body of great height and majesty that transcends all worlds;
and because, among the two vehicles,
the first [vehicle] transcends all worldly paths of the five destinies.
Second, because it purifies supramundane roots of goodness;
"the Buddha exhausts a single phrase" means that one attains entry into the fulfillment of the wisdom of an omniscient person.
Because its own power, eloquence, and comparative excellence are supreme among the highest;
herein the Buddha exhausts a single phrase.
This is not present in the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* (Daben jing), nor is it found in the extant versions of this sūtra.
There are two phrases regarding the eloquence of other-power:
first, because of the spiritual power of all Buddhas;
second, because you are capable of receiving the Tathāgata’s power of wisdom.
These two phrases exist in the commentary on the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* but are not present in the sūtra itself;
they are combined into a single phrase.
There is one phrase for "other-power" (*parakrama*) and nine phrases for "self-power" (*svakrama*).

Based on the two phrases concerning the power of others (*parāśraya*) in the *Mahāvaipulya* [Sūtra] and the eight phrases concerning self-power (*svāśraya*), the sequence of chapters has already been explained;
next, the intention behind the additions will be discussed.
The treatise states:
There are ten kinds of mental applications.
Regarding the fearless body, there are two types:
first, the excellence of the form-body (*rūpakāya*).
The second is the excellence of the body (*kāyavaiśeṣya*). Regarding the excellence of the form-body (*rūpakāyavaiśeṣya*):
it is called the excellence of the body because, like a king among his assembly, it is truly and unsurpassed; there are nine kinds of this.
First, eloquence that is unattached,
because it possesses the eloquence of unhindered and joyful speech;
second, eloquence that is capable.
Fourth is the wisdom of capability, because it skillfully discriminates pure wisdom.
Regarding the four types of capability:
first is capability regarding causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).
Second, fitness of the factors;
third, fitness of the performance;
fourth, fitness of the accomplishment.

"Conditions" refers to knowing all conditioned collections of causes and conditions (*saṃskṛta-pratyaya-samudaya*) and unconditioned collections of causes and conditions (*asaṃskṛta-pratyaya-samudaya*), and so forth.
"Phenomena" refers to the entire realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), and so forth.
"Agent" refers to the dual application of both opposition and compliance.
To oppose it leads to birth and death;
to accord with it leads to nirvana.
Each of these two dharmas possesses two functions: that of opposition and that of accord.
The wisdom of enlightenment of one who has accomplished both [types of eloquence] is neither separate from nor detached from it;
even all the factors conducive to enlightenment accomplish nirvāṇa.
Third is the eloquence of unrestrained release.
It is said that [the first] is because one speaks without depending on a sequence and with uninterrupted speech due to excellent mindfulness and non-forgetfulness;
the fourth is the eloquence of being able to speak,
which is due to excellent, decisive wisdom.
Fifth is the eloquence of non-confusion,
because it reaches all states of omniscience.
Sixth is the eloquence of issuing forth instruction.
Because it is inseparable from the indestructible powers of all Buddhas;
seventh, the eloquence of fearlessness,
because it is inseparable from the intrepidities of all Buddhas.
Eighth is the eloquence of the eight immeasurables,
because it skillfully opens the gates of Dharma by discerning all phenomena through the unimpeded wisdom of the Buddhas.
Ninth is the eloquence of common transformation.
Because [the Buddha] possesses the supreme and wondrous bodily, verbal, and mental actions of all Buddhas.
Having already explained the empowerment of the mind,
the following ten phrases explain why he is worthy of such empowerment and thus bestows it.
For what reason do the Buddhas, through their compassionate tenfold body of fearlessness, bestow this [teaching] solely upon Vajragarbha and not upon others?
The explanation states:
because this bodhisattva has attained the dharma of the Mahāyāna-prabhāsvara-samādhi (the Samādhi of the Radiance of the Great Vehicle).
This is because others do not attain it.
There are two kinds of attainment of samādhi:
first, because the fulfillment of one’s original vow manifests before one.
This is also due to the power of the Bodhisattva’s original vows,
and because the body of samādhi encompasses meritorious qualities.
There are eight kinds of meritorious qualities encompassed by this body of samādhi.
This is because they pertain to one's own benefit and the benefit of others:
the first four concern one's own benefit,
while the latter four— retention through mindfulness and so forth— concern the benefit of others.
First, purity of cause, because the defiled mind has become direct and pure;
second, purity of wisdom, because wisdom is clear and bright;
third, purity of the transformation of the body, because the factors that aid the path have been well accumulated.
The fourth is because it is the fundamental karma for purifying the mind.
These four constitute self-benefit.
The fifth is the purification through hearing, which consists of retaining immeasurable teachings through mindfulness.
Sixth, because of the pure light of the Dharma through the purity of faith and understanding of the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*).
Seventh, because of the purity of eloquence (*pratibhāna*) through the indestructible attainment of the gateways of *dhāraṇī*.
Eighth, because of the purity of freedom from pride; "purity" here refers to wisdom (*jñāna*).
Because the Dharma-realm wisdom-seal is well-sealed.
Having already explained the empowerment of speech,
what is the empowerment of body?
The phrase "extending the hand" and below clarifies the signs of the bodily empowerment (*kāyādhiṣṭhāna*).
The treatise states:
"Without leaving one's original place."
As for the act of stroking the crown of the head,
it is intended to manifest a particularly sublime supernatural power;
this is the supernormal power of *ṛddhi* (psychic potency), not any other such power.
The section on the "Augmenting Factors" has been explained.
Next, the section on the "Arising" is explained. The treatise says:
"As for 'arising from samādhi'..."
Because the matter of samādhi has been concluded,
and because he has attained superior power; furthermore,
when it is time to speak, he enters a state of meditative concentration in which there is no verbal expression.
The section on origination has already been explained.
Next, the section on the fundamental [nature] will be explained.
This follows the section on origination within this chapter.
The second part is the actual exposition of the text. Why is it not spoken?
If one does not speak oneself, the assembly will not know whether it is being taught or not.
Furthermore, it is not known what specific teaching is about to be expounded.
Within the formal exposition itself, there are five sections.
The first is a general presentation of the essence of the Dharma, arising from within the *dharmatā* realized by the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
Second, regarding the enumeration of the ten numbers based on the undifferentiated dharma, it is likewise praised as being identical throughout the three periods of time.
Third, regarding the listing of the names below the enumeration, they are likewise praised as being identical throughout the three periods of time.
Fourth, from "having thickly accumulated roots of goodness" onwards, the detailed explanation is also identical throughout the three periods of time.
The fifth is the final bond, which consists of ten meanings.
Having accumulated the roots of goodness extensively, as previously established in the various assemblies,
there is a total accumulation, a total stabilization, and a total augmentation.
Up to the point where the general number and general invocation are presented,
the sections from "thickly accumulated" (*saṃbhṛta*) onwards provide a detailed explanation of the specific, the added, the invoked, and the revealed meanings of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
Within the initial general presentation of the essence of the Dharma, there are six kinds of certainties.
Among these, the aspiration for perfect determination is the general [category],
as it is the bodhicitta itself;
the others are the specific [categories].
The determination of their common characteristics;
"distinctive characteristics" refers to their specific characteristics;
"established characteristics" is a brief explanation.
The characteristic of disintegration is the extensive explanation;
thus, there are six kinds of determination.
First is the determination of the excellence of the observed characteristic.
2. True and virtuous determination;
3. Superior virtuous determination;
4. Causal virtuous determination.
There are five kinds of excellent determination regarding the great elements,
and the sixth is the excellent determination of being free from cowardice;
there is no one who surpasses these.
This refers to the "well-determined observation of characteristics.
The *Treatise* states:
"Because the contemplation of True Suchness has the characteristic of a single flavor."
That which is indestructible is precisely the true, virtuous, and definitive.
As the treatise states:
That which is not the realm of the world yet is the world,
as vast as the *dharmadhātu*,
is the supreme, virtuous certainty.
The treatise says:
"Because the Great Dharma-realm is the fundamental source of the Buddha,
it is ultimately like empty space."
This refers to "well-determined by cause.
The treatise states:
"There are two kinds."
It is a cause for the fruit of impermanent attachment that is established once and for all.
This cause is like space, for it is inexhaustible as it gives rise to all forms.
It persists until the end of the future.
The Treatise states:
"Because one attains the path to nirvāṇa through constant causes and fruits.
This single phrase is missing from the Mahāvaipulya Sūtra.
That which follows "having completely covered all" is the Great Determination of Excellence (*mahākuśalaviniścaya*).
The treatise states:
"Because it accords with conduct that benefits others."
Why is this? The following refers to the sixth [quality], "skillful determination without timidity.
The treatise states:
"Because one enters the ground of wisdom of all Buddhas of the three periods of time."
"What are they? and below this is the second section, which provides a general enumeration of ten items.
"What are the ten items? and below this is the third section, which lists the names individually.
The treatise states:
"In contrast to the ten obstacles, the ten names arise.
This section has two parts.
First, the enumeration of names;
second, the explanation beginning with "For what reason," which constitutes the accomplishment of the two practices.
It is called "Joy" because one first realizes the state of sainthood;
it is called "Freedom from Defilement" because one is free from the mind that violates the precepts through awakening;
it is called the "Luminous Ground" because the Dharma is manifested through the illumination of the three kinds of wisdom.
Because the fire of wisdom burns the fuel of afflictions, it is called the Blazing Ground (Arciṣmatī-bhūmi).
Because of the skillful means of supramundane wisdom, it is called the Difficult to Conquer Ground (Sudurjayā-bhūmi).
Because great wisdom manifests before one, it is called the Manifest Ground (Abhimukhī-bhūmi).
Because the ultimate perfection of signless practice enables one to transcend the stages of the two vehicles, it is called the "Far-Reaching Stage" (Dūraṃgamā-bhūmi).
Because retributive practice has become fully matured and is signless without distinction, it is called "Immovable" (Acalā-bhūmi).
Because of the power of unimpeded eloquence in preaching the Dharma, it is called "Excellent Intelligence" (Sādhumatī-bhūmi).
Because he has attained the Great Dharma-body and is fully endowed with sovereign mastery, he is called "Dharmamegha" (Cloud of Dharma).
From the passage beginning "In silence," the fourth section contains two parts.
The first clarifies that after Vajragarbha had finished speaking, he remained silent to inspire reverence in the assembly and cause them to honor the Dharma.
Regarding the second point, from the section on Vimukticandra onwards, the text clearly explains the request for the teaching. First, concerning the initial silence, there are four intentions.
The treatise states:
"First, it is because he wishes to cause the great assembly to feel a thirsting longing so that they may request the teaching."
Second, it is because he wishes to cause the assembly to revere the person and honor the Dharma.
Third, he remains silent and does not speak because those who possess faith and understanding have expectations [for him to teach].
The fourth [section] concerns the request made at the Cloud Terrace (Meghadhvaja) to exhort the Buddha to bestow his grace; this is because the Buddha’s grace was added [to the teaching].
Within the second [section on] requests, Vimukticandra makes three requests:
the first consists of a prose section and five verses.
Two prose sections and two verses;
three prose sections and four and a half verses.
These are the answers of Vajragarbha.
The first consists of one prose section and six verses;
the next consists of one prose section and three verses.
These two respond to the request of Vimukticandra and the great assembly.
The first consists of prose and five and a half verses;
the Cloud Terrace [chapter] adds an exhortation.
The second consists of prose and seven and a half verses.
Vajragarbha answered Vimukticandra with one long prose section and six verses,
followed by a second long prose section and its corresponding verses.
The final prose section and verse respond collectively to the requests made by the great assembly and from the Cloud-Pavilion.
The initial prose section and five verses at the beginning of the Chapter on Liberation [respond] to the request of Śakra.
The treatise states:
"The first verse reveals the speaker,
because his pure awakening is free from fault."
The next verse reveals that the listeners share a certainty regarding the Dharma;
the subsequent verse demonstrates that the assembly delights in hearing it.
The following verse demonstrates that the rest of the assembly has purified their minds;
the subsequent verse reveals that this assembly has all examined and heard this [teaching].
Among these, the first verse praises the speaker.
The following two verses reveal the purity of the assembly of self-arisen ones;
the final verse reveals the purity of the two assemblies.
The Commentary states:
The first two verses inquire as to why [the Buddha] remained silent;
this is because the assembly now harbors doubts.
The final three verses clarify the purity and joy of the great assembly.
One should preach because of the earnest and reverent inquiry into the profound Dharma.
From the passage beginning with Vajragarbha, both the prose (*gadya*) and the verses (*śloka*) respond to the aforementioned request.
According to the commentary, the six verses that follow are explained based on the prose of the *Mahāvaipulya* version; they are not the six verses found in the original sūtra text itself.
To cause the assembly to rejoice, [the author] provides a general response regarding the characteristics [of the teaching].
Within the six verses of the original scripture,
the first clarifies the difficulty [of the practice], while the subsequent verse clarifies the difficulty [of the meaning].
These two verses together explain that which is difficult to speak; thus, one becomes bewildered and distressed.
The third and fourth verses clarify that which is difficult to hear:
it can only be heard by those who maintain their minds free from the notion of self.
The fifth verse uses a metaphor to clarify and establish the first objection.
The sixth verse clarifies that those who give rise to faith are few, thereby establishing the preceding objection regarding what is heard.
Alternatively, it may also be treated as two [separate points].
The first two verses and the fifth directly state the difficulty of teaching;
the third and fourth directly state the difficulty of hearing.
Although Liberation (Mokṣa) requested again, he still adhered to his previous position.
From "The two Buddha-sons" onwards is the section on hearing the difficult [teachings] atop the banner.
From "Having received the Buddha’s spiritual power" onwards is the section on expounding the difficult [teachings] atop the banner.
From "In this profound Dharma" onwards is the concluding section.
In the second invitation during the Jie tuo ri (Day of Liberation), the banners were returned to their positions above;
this was verified by inspection and hearing atop the banners since the time they were tied and obstructed.
The second [instance] was difficult to hear.
From "With a profound mind" (*gambhīracittena*) onwards, the fourth section concerns the fear arising from the production of faith;
from "One should rely on the Buddha’s spiritual power" (*buddhānubhāvam āgamya*) onwards, the second section provides a metaphorical illustration to explain the difficulty [of this faith];
and from "In this profound Dharma" (*asmin gambhīre dharme*) onwards, the first section concerns the confusion and the difficulty of explaining it, consisting of two lines of verse.
The first verse directly requests an examination of the difficulty regarding the discourse on the banner;
the subsequent verse establishes the examination of what was heard.
The treatise contains only the prose (*gadya*) and lacks the versified recitation (*gāthā*).
Next, regarding the repeated request:
it was stated above that those capable of providing verified testimony are difficult to find;
however, this assembly possesses the capacity for such verification. As for those with "well-purified profound minds," there are two kinds of profound mind in total.
First is the purity of the scriptures (āgama-viśuddhi);
second is the purity of realization (adhigama-viśuddhi).
There are five kinds of purity of the scriptures.
There are four kinds of verified purity (*avetyaprasāda*).
As for the five kinds:
first, purity through desire (*chanda-prasāda*).
Second, seeking purity;
third, purity through observance;
fourth, purity obtained by birth. Regarding these four kinds:
First, purity through attainment;
second, purity through non-engagement;
third, purity through insatiability.
Fourth is purity through not following the teachings of others.
Since these nine types of *āgama* do not correspond with the *Mahānidāna-sūtra*,
this is not an explanation based on the *āgamas*.
The four [sections] on the return of the banner also rely on these two meanings.
Second, the prose and verses of the *Vajragarbha* (Vajragarbha-parivarta) constitute the extensive version of the sutra (*Mahā-sūtra*).
According to the commentary on the treatise,
although there is the prose section (*gadya*), it lacks the three verses of the *geya* (repeated verse).
Within the prose section, there are two parts.
Regarding those who initially received the superior grade, they were without doubt and could be verified through their learning.
As for those who delighted in the lesser Dharma and below, they possessed middling and inferior degrees of doubt;
here, "deluded" (huò) refers to the confusion of the mind, while "doubtful" (yí) refers to hesitation.
I have compassion for these people;
therefore, I remain silent.
In the verse, the first one and a half lines summarize the superior grade.
The following one and a half verses resolve doubts.
The third section consists of the prose and verse of Vimukticandra’s request,
which comprises four and a half verses.
The prose section consists of four points:
first, it exhorts that there is benefit in speaking and no fault in not speaking;
second, from the phrase "For what reason? onwards, it describes how all Buddhas protectively mind [the practitioner].
Third, "For what reason" and below clarifies the fundamental [nature] of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
Fourth, "Therefore" and below concludes with an exhortation.
Within these beneficial verses:
The first verse praises the benefits described above;
the next verse explains the protection and mindfulness of all Buddhas;
and the following verse praises the fundamental nature of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
The fourth section is the exhortation to conclude,
which is omitted and not versified. Above,
it was explained that Vimukticandra, as the leader of the assembly of co-arisen beings, made his request.
This clarifies the request made by the great assembly.

Regarding the section beginning with "The empowerment of the Buddha’s release" (*śāstṛ-prasāda-adhiṣṭhāna*) and continuing through the "Cloud-Pavilion Empowerment" (*megha-vedikā-adhiṣṭhāna*), there are four parts to the commentary on the five and a half verses of the request for instruction.
Of these, the first two verses praise the speaker’s accomplishment of the power of realization (*adhigama-bala*) and the power of scripture (*āgama-bala*).
The first verse praises the eloquence of realized power (*adhigama-bala*).
The upper line of the second verse praises the eloquence of scriptural authority (*āgama-bala*).
The single verse following "the ten powers" (*daśabala*) praises both the eloquence of requesting [teachings] and the eloquence of providing further explanation (*punar-vyākhyāna*).
The second verse praises the assembly’s examination and acceptance;
the third consists of the scriptural authority (*āgama*) and realization (*adhigama*);
one line displays this by means of a simile.
The analogy illustrates that the great assembly’s seeking of the Dharma becomes increasingly profound;
the final line concludes the request.
This interpretation does not accord with the original text.
The subsequent commentary explains that the first three lines praise the virtues of the speaker, who should preach because he is endowed with both types of wisdom;
the next one and a half verses clarify the assembly’s examination and acceptance;
and the final line concludes with the request to teach.
In the preceding praise, the first line generally praises the two types of wisdom;
the next line specifically praises wisdom;
and the following three lines praise the perfection of merit, as verified by the teaching.
Within the Cloud Terrace (Yun-tai), there are two prose sections and seven and a half verses.
The prose section concerns the empowerment of the body, while the verses clarify the empowerment of speech.
Within the empowerment of the body, there are two types of bodies and eight types of activities.
For the beginner:
first is the light that is the mark of awakening to karma;
second is the incalculable [aeons] of the cause of karma.
Third is the activity of rolling up and extending, which universally illuminates this;
fourth is the activity of cessation, which [removes] the three evil realms;
fifth is the activity of subduing, which is not present in the Mahāvaipulya [sūtras].
6. The activity of reverent service is that which follows "having fully illuminated.
7. The activity of manifestation is "pervasive illumination.
8. The activity of requesting [the Dharma] is "at all times."
Regarding the two bodies:
first is the meteoric body that illuminates all things;
second is the solar disc body, which is the great radiance terrace.

First, the empowerment by means of the mind (*manas*) was explained; now follows the empowerment by means of one's own body (*kāya*). After the verses have been recited, there is the empowerment by means of speech (*vāc*).
This section consists of exactly eleven and a half lines, whereas the root treatise contains twenty lines.
The difference lies merely in the extent of detail.
Because the Buddha does not abandon his original vow and because his great compassion is supreme, he offers this further exhortation.
The Cloud Terrace (Yúntái) represents the pinnacle of harmonious moisture and lofty manifestation.
Its text consists of seven and a half gāthās,
containing five lines within.
The first two verses reveal the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
The following single verse reveals the purpose of that empowerment;
briefly, these open up three meanings.
The following two verses concern the benefits of hearing the Dharma at three stages.
The subsequent half-verse concerns the harm incurred by not hearing it.
The final two verses open up three meanings; the preceding [two] open up three meanings which constitute the essence of each stage (*bhūmi*).
Regarding the distinctions in the meaning of the practice of purifying the stages (*bhūmi*), this refers to the characteristics of the stages.
Within the two practices of hearing and benefiting, there are three parts;
the first half clarifies the benefit at the time of hearing.
Next is the benefit at the time of practicing the half-lineage;
next is the benefit at the time of being born into the single lineage.
Among the latter three meanings, "the power of the practice upon entering the stages" refers to the fruit.
The contemplation of phenomena (*dharmānupaśyanā*) is fulfillment.
This briefly elucidates six meanings;
according to the treatise, there are four oral augmentations (*mukhākṣepa*).
The first one and a half lines reveal the one who bestows the empowerment;
that is, because the Buddha, the World-Honored One, the Dharma King, has accomplished four kinds of excellence.
First, the excellence of mastery.
Second, superiority of power;
third, superiority of retinue;
fourth, superiority of nature.
Regarding "the Peerless One":
among the Buddhas, the Dharmas, and sentient beings, there is none who can be equaled;
therefore, he is called the Peerless One.
This is because this [Dharmakāya] and that [Dharmakāya] are equal.
Second, two and a half lines reveal the purpose for which the addition was made.
Third, three lines reveal that there are three periods of benefit from teaching the Dharma to benefit others.
